title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 20: Makati City v. Civil Service Commission: Are Government Employees Entitled to an 'Automatic' Leave of Absence?
keywords: City Government of Makati v. Civil Service Commission
kidnapping for ransom with physical injuries
Section 35 of the Civil Service Rules
University of the Philippines v. Civil Service Commission
public office is a public trust
primary_topics: Chapter 20 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's vigorous Dissent in City Government of Makati v. Civil Service Commission and Eugenia Galzote, against the majority holding that a detained employee charged with a non-bailable offense need not file a leave application and cannot be dropped from the rolls.

His central legal contention that neither the Civil Service Law (EO 292) nor the CSC Rules provides for an 'automatic' leave of absence, so an employee absent at least thirty days without approved leave is AWOL and must be dropped from the service.

His refusal to accept the majority's excuses: incarceration did not prevent Galzote from writing to her employer, her 'suspension' was void because no administrative investigation was pending, and in any case preventive suspension lasts only ninety days.

The epilogue's judicial policy of upholding public service -- that public servants cannot simply 'disappear' and then claim circumstances beyond their control, and that the Makati government, having had nothing to do with her incarceration, should not pay for it.
sub_topics: CJP frames the two questions: must a civil service employee detained for a non-bailable offense still file a formal leave application, and may one who fails to do so be validly dropped from the rolls?
He records that Justice Josue N. Bellosillo, writing for a divided Court, answered both in the negative, and that he 'filed a vigorous Dissent.'

The facts: Galzote, a Makati clerk charged with kidnapping for ransom with physical injuries, was detained, suspended from September 9, 1991, dropped from the rolls effective January 21, 1993, acquitted on September 22, 1994, and sought reinstatement on October 19, 1994.
The CSC ordered her reinstated as Clerk III with back wages from October 19, 1994 and the Court of Appeals sustained it; Makati elevated the case arguing she was AWOL and was not denied due process.

The ponencia's reasoning, reproduced at length: the employer's own suspension order was the 'equivalent of a prior approval' of leave; notice should have been sent to the Rizal Provincial Jail; and the CSC, as the constitutionally mandated central personnel agency, may read an 'automatic leave of absence' into its own rules.

The ponencia's force-majeure analogy -- illness excuses prior application under Section 20, and other events beyond the employee's control such as being kidnapped or arrested are 'akin to predicaments of illness' -- plus its reliance on UP v. CSC, Re: Pedro P. Tiongson and Macabuhay v. Manuel.

The separate votes: Justice Kapunan concurred against 'a too-strict interpretation of the law' and the idea that judges are 'automatons'; Justice Vitug concurred but voted to limit back salaries to five years.

CJP's first ground: the Rules make no distinction and give 'no regard for the reason for the absence' -- Section 35 says employees absent at least thirty days without approved leave are AWOL and shall be dropped after due notice.

Section 20 makes approval of leave for any reason other than illness contingent on the needs of the service, so approval 'cannot be presumed' and an application must be filed before exceeding thirty days.

He stresses that Galzote filed no application of any kind, and that although she could not physically report, 'there was nothing to stop her from writing to the petitioner' -- 'an incarcerated person is not prevented from communicating with the outside world.'

He invokes the public interest: 'The government cannot be left in the lurch,' public office is a public trust, and a position cannot be left vacant indefinitely for an employee who 'just disappears without a word.'

Reading Section 60 of EO 292, he argues the only leave an employee is entitled to is one 'provided by law and the rules,' with the grant subservient to the 'interest of the service'; between an interpretation that prejudices the service and one that enhances it, the latter should prevail.

He answers the 'useless ceremony' charge: an application for leave 'is not a mere formality' but is essential to the delivery of public service, else efficiency 'will depend on the whim of the individual employee.'
He separates acquittal from employment: the criminal charge was not the reason for her loss of work -- 'she was dropped from the rolls because she was AWOL.'

He distinguishes the cited precedents: Gonzales involved superiors refusing to act on a filed application and never passed on automatic leaves; UP v. CSC -- a decision he himself wrote -- turned on academic freedom and on the employer wanting to keep the teacher, whereas here 'it is the unwanted employee who is insisting on her employment.'

On the suspension: under Bangalisan v. Court of Appeals preventive suspension is valid only as an incident of a pending administrative investigation, so her 'suspension' was void; and even if valid, Section 52 caps it at ninety days, after which she should have applied for leave.

On due process: with no leave application on file the city had no record of her whereabouts, a public corporation cannot be expected to track one of thousands of employees, and under Quezon v. Borromeo the written notice is 'not jurisdictional in nature.'

The Epilogue: the Ethical Standards Law requires 'utmost integrity and strictest discipline'; the 'tear-jerking rhetoric' about untold sufferings is misplaced since Makati had nothing to do with her jailing and she was acquitted 'on reasonable doubt'; compensation, if due, should come from whoever maliciously prosecuted her.
signature_phrases: an application for leave is not a mere formality; it is not a 'useless ceremony' as the majority calls it
the efficiency of public service will depend on the whim of the individual employee
The government cannot be left in the lurch
In short, she was dropped from the rolls because she was AWOL
ignorance of the law excuses no one from compliance therewith
So, how can a leave be ever automatic, especially here where no application was even filed?
I believe that the better policy is to uphold public service, discipline and integrity
No work, no pay. No application, no approval. No leave, no benefits.

stances.claim: There is no such thing as an 'automatic' leave of absence: neither the Civil Service Law nor the CSC Rules provides for one, and Section 35 makes any employee absent at least thirty days without approved leave AWOL, without regard to the reason for the absence.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual argument from the rules -- the regulation 'makes no distinction or qualification' -- reinforced by Section 20's needs-of-the-service condition

stances.claim: Detention did not excuse Galzote from applying, because an incarcerated person can still communicate with the outside world and she retained the capacity to inform her employer that she was still interested in her job.
stances.rhetorical_move: capability rebuttal: conceding she could not report physically while denying that she could not write

stances.claim: An application for leave is not a 'useless ceremony' but is essential to the proper delivery of public service, since absolute discretion to be absent would make efficiency depend on the whim of the individual employee.
stances.rhetorical_move: direct reply to the majority's own phrase, recast as a public-service consequence

stances.claim: Her acquittal is irrelevant to her employment, because she lost her job not for the pending criminal case but for years of unexplained absence without approved leave.
stances.rhetorical_move: causal separation of the criminal case from the administrative ground

stances.claim: The better policy is to uphold public service, discipline and integrity -- no work, no pay; no application, no approval; no leave, no benefits -- because the rule of law requires no less.
stances.rhetorical_move: epilogue in parallel maxims, elevating the dispute into a rule-of-law principle

notable_anecdotes: CJP states plainly that against Justice Bellosillo's ponencia for a divided Court he 'filed a vigorous Dissent,' and organizes the chapter as ruling-then-dissent.

He notes that University of the Philippines v. Civil Service Commission, the precedent the majority used against him, was 'a Decision I had the honor of writing,' and then explains why it does not apply.
He answers the majority's claim that expecting a 'lowly clerk' to know her suspension was void is 'too harsh' with the flat reply that ignorance of the law excuses no one.
He calls the majority's line about her 'untold sufferings and privations' in jail 'tear-jerking rhetoric' and asks why an employer with nothing to do with her incarceration should pay for it.
He points out that she was acquitted 'on reasonable doubt,' not on a finding that she did not participate in the crime, and directs any claim for compensation at whoever 'maliciously prosecuted' her.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 20 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' sets out Panganiban's dissent in City Government of Makati v. Civil Service Commission and Eugenia Galzote, which asked whether a civil servant detained on a non-bailable charge must still file a leave application and may be dropped from the rolls if she does not. Galzote, a Makati clerk charged with kidnapping for ransom with physical injuries, was suspended from September 9, 1991, dropped from the rolls effective January 21, 1993, acquitted in September 1994, and ordered reinstated with back wages by the CSC, which the Court of Appeals sustained. Writing for a divided Court, Justice Bellosillo held that the employer's own suspension order was the equivalent of prior approval of leave, that notice sent to her house was insufficient, and that the CSC could reasonably read an 'automatic leave of absence' into its rules for events of force majeure akin to illness; Justices Kapunan and Vitug concurred. Panganiban dissented. He argued that neither the Civil Service Law (EO 292) nor the CSC Rules provides for automatic leave; Section 35 makes thirty days' absence without approved leave AWOL regardless of reason, and Section 20 makes approval contingent on the needs of the service, so it 'cannot be presumed.' Detention was no excuse, since 'there was nothing to stop her from writing' to her employer, and 'the government cannot be left in the lurch.' An application, he insisted, 'is not a mere formality; it is not a useless ceremony,' else public efficiency would 'depend on the whim of the individual employee.' Her acquittal was beside the point: 'she was dropped from the rolls because she was AWOL.' He distinguished Gonzales and his own UP v. CSC, held her void suspension excused nothing beyond ninety days, and closed on public service and the rule of law: 'No work, no pay. No application, no approval. No leave, no benefits.'
